The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation is the largest philanthropic organization in the United States devoted solely to health. Based in Princeton, New Jersey, it was established in 1936 by Robert Wood Johnson II, a longtime leader of the health care products company Johnson & Johnson. When he died in 1968, he left most of his company stock to the foundation, transforming it into a national force in philanthropy.

Over the decades, the foundation has focused on improving access to quality care, reducing the harm caused by unhealthy behaviors, and strengthening public health systems. Early efforts supported emergency medical services, including the creation of the 911 emergency system in many communities, and expanded the training of nurse practitioners. Later campaigns targeted tobacco use, childhood obesity, and substance abuse, contributing to measurable declines in smoking rates and growing national attention to nutrition and physical activity.

In recent years, the foundation has emphasized building a "culture of health," an approach recognizing that wellbeing depends not only on medical care but also on housing, education, income, and community conditions. It has committed itself to addressing structural racism and health disparities, arguing that fair opportunity is essential to good health.

Through grants, research, and policy partnerships, the foundation continues to shape national conversations about health. Its long history demonstrates how sustained private philanthropy can influence public policy and improve lives.

Great question! While the SIPC is a non-profit membership corporation and not a government agency, it is highly unlikely to go bankrupt in the traditional sense due to significant legislative safeguards.

The SIPC is primarily funded by assessments paid by its member broker-dealers. If this fund were to be depleted during a major market crisis, the SIPC has a $5 billion line of credit with the U.S. Treasury, accessible through the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Furthermore, under the Securities Investor Protection Act (SIPA), the SEC has the authority to lend money to the SIPC if it is necessary for the protection of customers.

Because the SIPC is a critical component of U.S. financial market stability, it operates with a substantial government backstop. While no entity is technically "invincible," the federal government's ability to provide emergency funding makes a total SIPC insolvency extremely improbable. In a scenario where the SIPC's resources and its multi-billion dollar Treasury line were both exhausted, it would likely signify a systemic financial collapse, at which point Congress would almost certainly intervene to restore market confidence.

So, while it is technically a private entity, its deep ties to the Treasury provide a safety net that standard corporations simply do not have.

Short answer: it depends on the rice, but the classic absorption method + rinsing/soaking is the most versatile and foolproof if you want fluffy, separate grains. Quick rundown from my kitchen experiments:

1) Rinse first (unless you want creamy/starchy rice like risotto). Put the rice in a bowl or fine-mesh sieve and rinse under cold water until it runs mostly clear. This removes excess surface starch and prevents clumping.

2) Ratio and timing (general guides):

- Long-grain white (jasmine): about 1 cup rice: 1.25-1.5 cups water. Bring to a boil, cover, simmer very low 10-12 minutes, then remove from heat and rest 10 minutes.

- Basmati: rinse, soak 20-30 minutes if you have time, then use ~1: 1.5 water, same cook/rest routine. Soaking helps it get long fluffy grains.

- Short-grain (sushi): ~1: 1.1-1.2. Rinse well.

- Brown rice: ~1: 2.25-2.5, simmer 35-45 minutes, rest 10 minutes.

These ratios can vary by brand and how much chew you like, so think of them as starting points.

3) The method: use a heavy-bottomed pot with a tight-fitting lid. Bring pot to a boil uncovered, give it a quick stir, then reduce to the lowest flame, cover, and don't lift the lid. The trapped steam finishes cooking. After the timer, leave it covered and let it rest — that final steam step is crucial.

4) Extras: a pinch of salt and a teaspoon of butter or oil improves flavor and keeps grains separate. For separate grains, briefly toast rice in oil first (pilaf method) before adding water. For sticky/glutinous rice, soak for hours and steam instead of boiling.

5) Rice cooker or Instant Pot: if convenience matters, these are great — follow the machine's cup markings. Instant Pot excels for brown rice.

Troubleshooting: too soggy → drain and spread to dry a bit, or cook uncovered. Too firm → add a splash of hot water, cover, and steam a few minutes.

Personally I do jasmine 1:1.25, rinse, low simmer 12 minutes, rest 10 — always fluffy. But ultimately match method to rice type and you'll be golden.

Imagine your body as a city and your immune system as its security team. Germs like viruses and bacteria are intruders trying to sneak in, cause chaos, and use your cells as factories to make more of themselves.

Your immune system has two main jobs: recognize what belongs to you, and attack what doesn't. When a new germ shows up, your body doesn't immediately know how to fight it. Special cells have to study the intruder, figure out what makes it unique (like its "face" or uniform), and then design weapons—usually antibodies—to target it. This learning process works, but it can take days, during which you might get sick.

Vaccines basically act like a training simulator for your immune system.

Every September, teachers across the country spend weeks re-teaching material students already learned the previous spring. This problem, often called summer learning loss, is one of the strongest arguments for year-round schooling. Although the idea of giving up a three-month summer break sounds miserable to most students, a balanced year-round calendar would benefit students, families, and teachers.

The main advantage is retention. Researchers have long found that students, especially in math, lose some of their skills during long breaks. Year-round schools keep the same number of instructional days but spread them out, with shorter breaks every couple of months. Students stay in the habit of learning, and teachers can move forward instead of constantly reviewing.

Year-round schooling also addresses inequality. Wealthier families can afford summer camps, tutors, and trips that keep their kids engaged. Lower-income students often lack those options, and the gap between them widens each summer. A shorter break narrows that gap by giving every student more consistent access to school, which also provides meals and a safe place to be.

Critics argue that students need a long summer to rest and that year-round schedules disrupt family plans and summer jobs. These concerns are fair, but burnout is arguably more likely during long stretches without a break, and shorter, more frequent vacations give students time to recharge throughout the year. Families would still be able to travel, just at different times.

Education should be built around how people actually learn, not around a calendar designed for farming communities more than a century ago. Switching to year-round schooling would be an adjustment, but it is one worth making.

# How Neural Networks Learn

Okay so imagine you're teaching a kid to recognize dogs. You don't give them a rulebook that says "if it has four legs and fur, it's a dog." Instead, you just show them a bunch of pictures and say "that's a dog, that's a dog, that's not a dog, that's a dog." Eventually their brain figures out the pattern on its own.

Neural networks learn basically the same way, except instead of a kid's brain, it's a computer program that's trying to recognize patterns in data.

Here's how it actually works: A neural network starts out completely clueless. It's basically a bunch of mathematical functions all strung together, and all the settings in those functions are just random garbage at first. When you feed it an image of a dog, it makes a guess about what it is. Spoiler alert: the guess is usually wrong because it hasn't learned anything yet.

So you tell it what the right answer was. "Nope, that's a dog, not a cat." Then—and this is the cool part—the network looks back at all those mathematical functions and tweaks them slightly. It's like saying, "Okay, I was wrong, so I need to adjust my thinking a tiny bit so that next time I'm more likely to get this right."

Your eyes are like cameras and your brain is like a computer. We *both* learn that a certain kind of light is called "red."

We can't climb into each other's brains to see if it "looks" the same, but:

- Our eyes are built very similarly.

- We can test them: we point at the same apple, stoplight, or crayon and both say "red."

- Colorblind people show us what happens when the eye wiring is different.

So we don't know if red *feels* identical in our minds, but we know we're talking about the same thing in the world.

Europe has a reputation for being expensive, and honestly, parts of it are. But after a few trips where I counted every euro, I've learned that you can see a lot without emptying your bank account. Here's what actually worked for me.

First, pick your destinations wisely. Western Europe is gorgeous, but Paris, Amsterdam, and Zurich will eat your budget fast. Eastern and Southern Europe are where your money stretches. Think Lisbon, Krakow, Budapest, Sofia, or Belgrade. A great meal in Krakow might cost you what a sandwich does in Copenhagen, and the cities are every bit as beautiful.

Second, travel in shoulder season. May, early June, September, and October have fewer crowds, cheaper flights, and lower accommodation prices. You'll also dodge the brutal summer heat in places like Rome and Seville, which is a bonus.

Getting around is easier than you'd think. Budget airlines like Ryanair and Wizz Air sometimes offer flights for less than a pizza, though watch out for baggage fees. Pack light and bring just a backpack. Overnight buses and trains can also save you a night of accommodation, though I'll admit I don't always sleep well on them. Once you're in a city, walk as much as you can. It's free, and you'll stumble onto things you'd never find on a metro.

For sleeping, hostels are still the classic choice, and many have private rooms if dorms aren't your thing. Look for ones with free breakfast and a kitchen. Cooking even a couple of meals a week adds up to real savings. Guesthouses and family-run pensions can also be surprisingly affordable outside the big tourist hubs.

Eating cheaply doesn't mean eating badly. Hit up local markets, bakeries, and lunch specials. In a lot of countries, the midday menu is a fraction of the dinner price. And skip restaurants with menus right next to major landmarks. Walk two streets over and you'll pay less for better food.

Finally, lean into free stuff. Many cities offer free walking tours (tip your guide), free museum days, and parks with incredible views. Some of my best memories came from sitting on a hillside with a cheap bottle of wine and a sunset.

Budget travel isn't about deprivation. It's about spending on what matters and skipping the rest.

# Insights for Practice and Scholarship of Organizational Management

The field of organizational management stands at a critical juncture, requiring both practitioners and scholars to interrogate fundamental assumptions that have long guided their work. This intersection of practice and scholarship reveals significant gaps that demand urgent attention and reconceptualization.

Contemporary management theory has traditionally emphasized rational decision-making, hierarchical structures, and measurable outcomes. However, empirical evidence increasingly demonstrates that organizations operate within complex, often irrational systems where human factors, context, and emergence play dominant roles. The scholarship-practice divide perpetuates this disconnect: academics publish findings in journals rarely read by practitioners, while managers employ intuition-based strategies unsupported by rigorous research. This schism undermines both domains.

A critical examination reveals that much management scholarship remains reductionist, attempting to isolate variables in controlled settings that bear little resemblance to organizational reality. Studies emphasizing quantifiable metrics often overlook the qualitative dimensions—organizational culture, power dynamics, and informal networks—that fundamentally shape behavior and outcomes. Meanwhile, practitioners increasingly recognize that sustainable competitive advantage derives not from operational efficiency alone but from adaptive capacity, psychological safety, and genuine stakeholder engagement.

The scholarship-practice gap particularly manifests in leadership studies. Prevalent models focus on individual heroic leaders making rational decisions, yet real-world evidence suggests distributed leadership, collective intelligence, and contextual responsiveness matter profoundly. Organizations achieving genuine transformation typically involve entire systems, not charismatic individuals.

San Francisco is unusual in American government because it is both a city and a county, so its budget combines municipal and county functions. The city's annual budget, which has exceeded $14 billion in recent years, funds public health, transportation, policing, housing, and social services. With roughly 30,000 employees, it is among the largest per-capita budgets in the nation.

The General Fund, typically around $6 to $7 billion, is the discretionary portion of the budget. It draws mainly from property taxes, business taxes, sales taxes, hotel taxes, and transfer taxes on real estate transactions. Other revenues come from enterprise departments such as the Port, the Airport, the Municipal Transportation Agency, and the Public Utilities Commission. These operate largely on fees and charges rather than tax dollars.

The budget process is structured and public. The mayor submits a proposed budget to the Board of Supervisors by June 1, and the Board's Budget and Appropriations Committee reviews it, holds hearings, and may adjust spending before final approval in July. San Francisco budgets on a two-year cycle, which encourages longer-term planning, and the Controller's Office issues revenue projections and fiscal reports that guide decisions. The city also maintains reserves, including a rainy day reserve, to cushion against downturns.

Voter-approved measures strongly shape the budget. Proposition-driven set-asides require minimum spending on areas such as children's services, libraries, and transit, which limits flexibility. Under California's Proposition 13, property tax growth is capped, constraining local revenue, while new taxes generally require voter approval.

Recent challenges are significant. Remote work reduced downtown office occupancy and weakened commercial property values, hotel revenue, and sales tax receipts, contributing to projected deficits in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Rising labor costs, homelessness response, and behavioral health needs add pressure. The city has responded with spending restraint, hiring slowdowns, and efforts to revitalize downtown.

If you imagine sunlight as a white beam, it's actually made of all the colors of the rainbow mixed together. When that light hits our atmosphere, it runs into tiny particles—mostly nitrogen and oxygen molecules. These are much smaller than the wavelength of visible light, and that's the key.

Light of different colors has different wavelengths. Red and orange have longer wavelengths; blue and violet have shorter ones. The shorter the wavelength, the more it gets bounced around when it hits those tiny air molecules. This bouncing is called Rayleigh scattering.

As sunlight passes through the atmosphere, the blue and violet components of the light get scattered in all directions, like they're being sprayed around the sky. Red and yellow light mostly keep going in a straight line. Even though violet is scattered even more than blue, our eyes are less sensitive to violet, and some of that violet light gets absorbed higher up. So what we mostly perceive is blue, spread out evenly across the dome of the sky.

When the sun is low—sunrise or sunset—the light has to travel through a thicker slice of the atmosphere. More blue light gets scattered out of your direct line of sight, leaving more of the reds and oranges to reach your eyes.

Predicting the three-dimensional structure of proteins from primary amino acid sequences is a foundational challenge in computational biology. The emergence of transformer-based architectures has catalyzed a paradigm shift in this field, surpassing traditional folding methods by effectively capturing long-range dependencies. By utilizing self-attention mechanisms, these models extract complex evolutionary information and spatial constraints from large-scale genomic datasets. This study evaluates the integration of transformers in state-of-the-art systems such as AlphaFold2, highlighting how multi-head attention facilitates the mapping of co-evolutionary signals into precise geometric coordinates. We demonstrate that these models achieve near-experimental accuracy across diverse protein folds, significantly accelerating structural characterization and therapeutic design. Our analysis confirms that transformer architectures represent a transformative leap in decoding the sequence-to-function relationship in proteomics.

Imagine a neural network as a huge set of tiny decision-makers wired together, like a classroom of students passing notes. Each connection between them has a number attached — a weight — that controls how strongly one neuron listens to another. When you show the network a picture or some data, it's like whispering a question into the classroom: the input travels through the connections, the neurons combine the signals, and the network gives an answer.

At first the answers are mostly wrong because the weights are random. So we tell the network the correct answer and measure how far off it was — that's the error. Learning is simply adjusting the weights to reduce that error.

Europe has a reputation for being expensive, but with smart planning, you can explore it on a shoestring. The secret lies in choosing where, when, and how you travel.

Start with your destination. Western capitals like Paris, London, and Amsterdam drain wallets quickly, while Eastern and Southern Europe offer incredible value. Budapest, Krakow, Lisbon, and Sofia deliver stunning architecture, rich history, and excellent food at a fraction of the cost. A hearty meal in Poland can cost less than a coffee in Switzerland.

Timing matters just as much. Visit in shoulder season, April to May or September to October, when flights and accommodation drop in price and crowds thin out. You'll enjoy pleasant weather without the summer markup.

Getting around is easier than you might think. Budget airlines like Ryanair and Wizz Air sometimes offer fares under twenty euros, though watch out for baggage fees and pack light. Overnight trains and long-distance buses such as FlixBus save you a night's accommodation while covering serious ground. Within cities, walking is free and often the best way to discover hidden corners.

For lodging, hostels remain a classic choice, and many offer private rooms at reasonable rates. Consider house-sitting, guesthouses, or booking apartments with kitchens so you can cook some meals yourself.

Speaking of food, eat like a local. Skip tourist-trap restaurants near major landmarks and head to markets, bakeries, and lunch specials. Many museums also offer free entry on certain days, and free walking tours operate in nearly every major city.

Budget travel isn't about sacrificing experiences. It's about spending intentionally, so every euro goes toward memories that last.

The world narrows to the radius of my workbench when I am hunched over a 1970s analog radio. What begins as a quick inspection of a frayed wire invariably dissolves into a four-hour odyssey. I don't notice the sun setting or the cooling of my forgotten tea; I only see the intricate architecture of copper and solder.

Restoration is a conversation with the past. I navigate circuit boards like a cartographer, tracing current paths to find where the signal died.

I lose whole afternoons wrenching in my driveway, sun slanting across a bicycle frame propped on a milk crate. At first it's a tangle of seized bolts, frayed cables, and mystery noises. I set down to diagnose: spin the wheel, listen for rubs, squeeze the brake lever. The work is granular—degumming a chain with a toothbrush, filing a warped rim until it coasts straight, coaxing grease into a one-penny-wide bearing with a syringe. Time doesn't exist then; only the patient geometry of spokes and tools and the small satisfactions of alignment.

Restoring bikes taught me to translate curiosity into method. A stubborn cone lock or an inexplicable wobble can be a puzzle you solve by isolating variables, testing hypotheses, and learning from failure. I read forums at midnight, sketched diagrams, and accepted that sometimes the solution is a replacement part or a different perspective.

I began fixing hand-me-downs for neighbors and gradually organized a weekend repair clinic at the community center.

The market for robotic snowblowers represents a burgeoning niche within home automation, requiring a precise STP strategy to ensure commercial viability. Market segmentation begins with geographic factors, focusing on regions with significant annual snowfall and cold climates. Demographically, the market is divided into high-income homeowners who value time, elderly residents who may lack the physical capability for manual labor, and tech-savvy "early adopters" who prioritize smart home integration.

Targeting efforts should prioritize affluent suburban homeowners and property management firms. These groups possess the disposable income to invest in high-end robotics and a strong desire to eliminate the labor-intensive chore of snow removal. By focusing on these high-value segments, companies can maximize their return on investment during the initial market entry phase while building brand loyalty among those most affected by winter weather.

Positioning is the final pillar, where the robotic snowblower is framed as the ultimate solution for winter safety and convenience. It is positioned as an autonomous, "set-and-forget" appliance that ensures property accessibility without human intervention. By emphasizing reliability, precision navigation, and physical ease, the product occupies a unique space as a necessary evolution in modern property maintenance, transforming a seasonal burden into a seamless, automated process.

# Why I Finally Quit Social Media

Honestly, I didn't think I'd ever be the person to quit social media. Like, I was that girl who'd check Instagram before getting out of bed and scroll through TikTok while doing homework. But after two years of college, I just... couldn't do it anymore.

It started small. I noticed I was spending literally three hours a day just mindlessly scrolling, and I had nothing to show for it except anxiety and a weird sense of FOMO. I'd see people's highlight reels and somehow feel like I was missing out on life, even when I was literally out having fun. How messed up is that? I'd be at parties or hanging with friends and still be thinking about what to post or how many likes I'd get.

The mental health aspect was real too. I became obsessed with likes and comments in a way that feels embarrassing to admit now.

The first time I took apart a broken radio, I was nine, and my mom found me on the garage floor at midnight surrounded by tiny screws. I had meant to spend ten minutes. Instead, six hours had vanished.

That still happens whenever I'm repairing electronics. I'll sit down at my desk with a dead game controller or a flickering lamp, and the world narrows to the problem in front of me. Is it a cracked solder joint? A worn capacitor? I follow the clues with a multimeter and a lot of patience. When the device finally hums back to life, the satisfaction feels almost unreal.

Last spring, I fixed my neighbor's vintage record player. She cried a little when it played her late husband's favorite album. I hadn't expected that. I realized then that I wasn't only fixing machines; I was giving people back small pieces of their lives.

Now I'm studying electrical engineering, hoping to design things that last and can be repaired rather than thrown away. Time still disappears when I work, but I've stopped worrying about it. Those lost hours are where I feel most like myself.

I used to think failure meant I wasn't cut out for something. Last semester, after bombing my first organic chemistry exam, I realized that belief was getting in my way more than the material was.

I had memorized reaction steps without understanding why they happened. The failure showed me exactly where my understanding was thin, something I never would have discovered by getting an easy A.

I think failure teaches best when we treat it as information rather than a verdict. Asking "What specifically went wrong?"

The summer before junior year, I froze in front of thirty second graders. I had signed up to teach coding at my local library, convinced I could translate my love of computers into something inspiring. But as their voices rose and questions tangled together, my lesson plan fell apart. One student whispered, "This is boring," and the rest drifted away to their tablets.

Walking home, I considered quitting. I'd always been the quiet kid who preferred debugging code to leading people. Yet that failure nagged at me like an unsolved bug. I spent the next week re‑writing everything: breaking concepts into games, adding visuals, and testing activities on my skeptical younger brother.

The following Saturday, I sat on the carpet with the kids instead of standing at the front. We turned loops into a dance routine and conditionals into "choose your own adventure" stories. Laughter, not boredom, filled the room. By the end of the summer, several students had built simple games—and asked if we could keep going.

I learned that leadership isn't about having the loudest voice; it's about listening, iterating, and refusing to abandon a problem, whether it's a stubborn program or a room full of restless children.

By removing the pressure to wear expensive brand-name clothing, schools can reduce bullying based on appearance and create a sense of equality. Furthermore, uniforms streamline the morning routine and minimize distractions, allowing students to focus entirely on their academics rather than their outfits. While some argue that uniforms stifle individuality, students can still express themselves through extracurricular activities and personal achievements. Ultimately, implementing a uniform policy promotes discipline, safety, and a unified school spirit. By prioritizing academic focus over fashion trends, schools ensure that every student has an equal opportunity to succeed.

Sunrise Bakeshop on Elm Street is celebrating after being named Best Local Bakery at this year's County Food Awards, a surprise many in town say was long overdue. Owner Maria Lopez, who opened the shop five years ago with a single oven and a dream, accepted the wooden rolling-pin trophy Sunday night and thanked her small team for "doing the work and keeping the oven warm."

Judges singled out Sunrise's sourdough loaves and sticky cinnamon buns for their "consistent quality and creative twists," but regulars say it's the friendly counter chats and weekday morning ritual that make the place special. "They know my order before I say it," laughed longtime customer Greg Harris, savoring a free sample handed out after the announcement.

Lopez says the award will help the bakery expand its community programs — including weekend baking classes for teens and a partnership with the local food pantry. Walking into the house after a seven-hour school day, most students don't feel a sense of relief; they feel the weight of a backpack full of three more hours of work. The debate over whether homework should be banned has been going on for years, but as student stress levels reach an all-time high, the answer is becoming clear. While the intention behind homework is to reinforce learning, the reality is that it often does the exact opposite by causing burnout and widening the gap between students.

The most obvious issue is mental health. High schoolers are told to balance academics, sports, clubs, and a social life, yet they are expected to sacrifice their sleep and downtime to finish busy work. When a student is staying up until midnight to finish a worksheet, they aren't actually "learning" anymore; they are just surviving. This leads to a total lack of motivation. Instead of being curious about a subject, students start to resent it because it's the thing keeping them from getting the rest they desperately need.

Beyond stress, there is a major issue with equity. Homework assumes that every student has a quiet place to study, a stable internet connection, and parents who have the time or knowledge to help them. But that isn't the reality for everyone. For a student who has to work a part-time job to help their family or look after younger siblings, a heavy homework load isn't just a challenge—it's an impossibility. When grades are heavily dependent on work done outside the classroom, we aren't testing a student's intelligence; we're testing their privilege.

Critics argue that homework builds "grit" or prepares us for the "real world." However, in the real world, most people get to leave their work at the office. If the goal of school is to prepare us for a healthy adulthood, we should be teaching balance, not constant exhaustion. A total ban might be a stretch, but the current system is definitely broken. We need to prioritize quality over quantity and give students their lives back. School should be a place where we learn, not a shadow that follows us home every single night.

# Why I Quit Social Media

For years, I told myself that social media was just a tool—something I controlled rather than something that controlled me. I checked my phone first thing in the morning and last thing before bed. I scrolled through feeds during meals, conversations, and moments that should have been fully present. I justified it as "staying connected" and "keeping up with friends," but deep down, I knew something wasn't right.

The breaking point came gradually, then all at once. I noticed I was comparing my life to carefully curated highlight reels. My self-worth fluctuated based on likes and comments. I felt anxious when I posted something and it didn't get immediate engagement. I was spending hours consuming content that left me feeling empty rather than enriched. Social media had transformed from a way to connect into a source of constant anxiety and inadequacy.

I realized I wasn't actually connecting with people anymore—I was performing for an audience. Real friendships were being neglected while I maintained shallow interactions with hundreds of acquaintances. I was so busy documenting moments that I wasn't actually experiencing them. A sunset wasn't beautiful until I'd found the right filter. A meal wasn't enjoyable until it was photographed and shared.

The algorithm kept me addicted by design. Every time I felt bored or lonely, my phone beckoned with notifications and endless content. Social media platforms employ teams of engineers specifically tasked with making their apps more addictive. Knowing this, I felt complicit in my own manipulation.

But what finally pushed me to delete the apps was recognizing how much time I was wasting. I calculated that I was spending roughly two hours daily scrolling. That's over 700 hours per year—entire weeks of my life—spent consuming content I wouldn't remember. What could I do with those hours instead? Learn a skill, read books, exercise, have meaningful conversations, pursue hobbies, spend time with family.

The first week without social media was surprisingly difficult. I reached for my phone dozens of times out of pure habit. But that discomfort quickly faded, replaced by genuine benefits. I slept better without the constant stimulation before bed. I had more patience and focus for deep work. Conversations became richer because I was fully present. I rediscovered boredom, which actually sparked creativity rather than panic.

Most importantly, I stopped comparing myself to others.

Edmund Gettier's short 1963 paper profoundly challenged the classical analysis of knowledge as justified true belief (JTB). By presenting concise counterexamples, Gettier showed that the three conditions—truth, belief, and justification—might all be met while intuitive knowledge is still absent. His ingenious scenarios involve agents holding justified beliefs that are true by luck rather than by the justificatory connection one expects for knowledge. In one case, justification rests on a false belief that accidentally yields a true conclusion; in another, defeasible reasoning leads to a lucky truth. These vignettes are deliberately minimal, revealing that justification and truth can come apart in ways that undermine the JTB account.

The significance of Gettier's argument lies not in its technical complexity but in its philosophical consequences. It forced epistemologists to acknowledge that a fourth condition—or a reconceptualization of existing conditions—is required to capture what we mean by "knowing." Subsequent responses have pursued several strategies. Some retain a JTB framework while adding constraints—no false lemmas, indefeasibility, or an anti-luck condition—to block Gettier-style cases. Others move away from internalist justification toward reliable belief-forming processes (reliabilism) or contextualist accounts that shift the standards for "knowing" with conversational context. Virtue epistemology reframes knowledge as arising from intellectual virtues rather than mere justification.

Beyond technical fixes, the Gettier problem stimulated deeper reflection on epistemic value: why is knowledge more epistemically valuable than mere true belief? It also sharpened attention to the links among evidence, inference, and luck. Whether one adopts a corrective condition or abandons JTB altogether, Gettier's intervention remains a foundational turning point, reshaping twentieth-century epistemology and continuing to motivate debates about the nature and standards of knowledge.

The Dram Shop Act represents a legislative effort to allocate responsibility for alcohol-related harm not only to intoxicated individuals but also to the commercial establishments that serve them. At its core, this law recognizes that bars, restaurants, and retail outlets occupy a strategic position in preventing alcohol-fueled injuries, particularly those arising from drunk driving and assaults. By imposing civil liability on vendors who sell alcohol to visibly intoxicated persons or minors, the Act aims to shift part of the social and economic burden of alcohol abuse onto those who profit from its sale.

Critically, the Dram Shop Act raises questions about fairness, foreseeability, and the balance between personal responsibility and corporate accountability. Supporters argue that alcohol vendors benefit from a potentially hazardous product and are often in the best position to interrupt dangerous chains of events. A bartender who continues serving someone staggering, slurring, and becoming belligerent can reasonably foresee the risk that person poses upon leaving the premises. In this sense, dram shop liability acts as a deterrent, incentivizing training, stricter internal policies, and vigilance in refusing service.

However, critics contend that the Act can overextend liability and encourage speculative litigation. It may be difficult to prove exactly when patrons became "visibly intoxicated" or whether a server should have recognized the danger. Moreover, placing too much legal weight on vendors can obscure individual autonomy: the choice to drink excessively and then drive remains the personal act of the intoxicated individual. There is also concern that the fear of lawsuits could push businesses to adopt discriminatory practices, such as disproportionately refusing service to certain demographic groups perceived as "risky."

Ultimately, the Dram Shop Act embodies a compromise between libertarian and paternalistic approaches to alcohol regulation. Its effectiveness depends on careful statutory drafting, consistent enforcement, and robust training for servers, striving to reduce alcohol-related harm while neither absolving individuals of responsibility nor unfairly burdening legitimate businesses.

It's not that it's a bad film—it's solidly made, well-acted, and looks great. The issue is how it's talked about like it's some daring, profound deconstruction of society and mental illness when it's mostly a collage of better, older movies (*Taxi Driver*, *King of Comedy*, etc.) with the serial numbers filed off.

The social commentary is about as subtle as a brick. The movie really wants to be about systemic failure—mental health funding, class resentment, alienation—but it never goes beyond surface-level "society bad" observations. It gestures at big ideas then retreats back into "crazy guy snaps and causes chaos" territory. That'd be fine if it were just a pulpy villain origin, but the way it's marketed and praised, you'd think it reinvented psychological drama.

Phoenix is excellent, but the character he's playing is written pretty thin. Arthur's transformation feels less like a tragic, inevitable descent and more like a series of plot checkpoints the movie knows it has to hit to get him into clown makeup by the finale. It leans hard on performance and atmosphere to cover up how little it has to actually say about him as a person beyond "abused, lonely, mentally ill, then violent."

The movie also flirts with the idea of being an "incel manifesto" or a critique of that mindset, but it never takes a stance. It just keeps things ambiguously edgy so people can project whatever reading they prefer. That's clever from a marketing standpoint, but dramatically it leaves the film feeling hollow. The ambiguity in *Taxi Driver* feels purposeful; the ambiguity in *Joker* often feels like hedging.

Stylistically, it borrows Scorsese's vocabulary—slow-burn build, city-as-hellscape, unreliable narrator—but without the same moral tension or complexity. In *Taxi Driver*, you're disturbed by how easy it is to start understanding Travis. In *Joker*, it's more like: "Here is a broken man, and here is the moment he breaks," with needle drops and slow-mo to signal when you should be shocked or hyped.

And that's really where the "overrated" part comes in. As an R-rated comic-book spinoff with a big performance at the center, it's pretty effective. But the pedestal it's been put on—as this deep, dangerous, conversation-changing masterpiece—feels disconnected from what's actually on screen. It's a decent movie with great acting that got treated like a cultural revolution.

Think of your immune system as a highly trained, slightly paranoid security team that lives inside your body. Their entire job is to spot intruders—like viruses or bacteria—and kick them out before they can cause a total system meltdown.

The problem is that when a brand-new virus shows up, your security team doesn't recognize it. They don't have a "Wanted" poster for it yet. So, while they're standing around trying to figure out if this new thing is a threat or just a piece of dust, the virus starts replicating like crazy. By the time the security team realizes they're under attack and starts building specific weapons to fight back, you're already miserable and stuck in bed.

A vaccine is basically a controlled training simulation. It's a way to show your security team what the enemy looks like without actually putting your body in danger.

Back in the day, vaccines usually used a "killed" or extremely weakened version of the virus. Nowadays, we have even cooler tech, like mRNA vaccines, which don't use the virus at all. Instead, they just give your cells a set of instructions—like a temporary recipe—to make a tiny, harmless piece of the virus (often called a "spike protein").

Whether it's an old-school vaccine or the new stuff, the result is the same: your immune system sees this "fake" intruder and goes into full red-alert mode. It studies the intruder, learns its weaknesses, and starts mass-producing specialized proteins called antibodies. These are like heat-seeking missiles designed to latch onto that specific virus and neutralize it.

More importantly, your body creates "memory cells." These are like the veteran guards who never forget a face. They file away the blueprint for those antibodies in a permanent folder.

This is why you sometimes feel a bit cruddy after a shot. If you get a sore arm, a mild fever, or feel tired, that's not the virus making you sick—because the virus isn't actually there. That's just your security team running the drill. They're sounding the alarms, heating up the building (fever), and using energy to build their defenses. It's proof that the training is working.

Once the training is over, your body cleans up the simulation materials and goes back to normal. But now, if the *real* virus ever tries to sneak in, your security team doesn't hesitate for a second. They recognize it instantly, pull the blueprints out of the file, and wipe the virus out before you even know you were exposed. You don't get sick because your body already won the war before it could even start.

Europe can be surprisingly affordable if you travel smart. Start by choosing where and when: eastern and southern Europe (Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, parts of the Balkans, Portugal) tend to be cheaper than Scandinavia, Switzerland or major Western capitals. Travel in shoulder seasons (April-May and September-October) to save on flights and accommodation while avoiding peak crowds.

Transport eats into budgets, so book smart. Long-distance night trains and buses are cost-effective—FlixBus covers wide routes and saves on a night's lodging; BlaBlaCar rideshares are cheap and flexible. Consider passes (Interrail/Eurail) only for intensive rail itineraries; point-to-point tickets can sometimes be cheaper if booked early. If you fly, factor in baggage and airport-transfer costs; budget airlines are great for quick hops but add up with fees.

Accommodation options beyond hotels include hostels (private rooms are often very reasonable), guesthouses, budget B&Bs, and short-term apartment rentals where cooking is possible. Couchsurfing and house-sitting are options if you're comfortable with them. Book ahead for festival-heavy periods; last-minute deals work best off-season.

Eat like a local: skip tourist restaurants and look for market stalls, bakeries, food halls, and lunchtime menu del día options in Spain or prix fixe lunches in France. Grocery stores (Lidl, Aldi, local markets) let you picnic in parks — a big money-saver. Street food or neighborhood eateries not only cut costs but give more authentic flavors.

Free and cheap attractions are everywhere: walking tours (tip-based), city passes that include public transit and major museums, free museum days, parks, churches and viewpoints. Scout opening hours—some museums have late openings on certain days or free-entry times. Use local transit daily passes, or simply walk: many European cities are compact and walkable.

Money and connectivity: use a bank card with low foreign-transaction fees, withdraw larger amounts to avoid ATM charges, and carry some cash for small vendors. If you need data, an eSIM or local SIM is usually cheaper than roaming unless your plan includes EU coverage.

Pack light to avoid baggage fees and to move easily between places. A daypack, good walking shoes, a reusable water bottle and a compact umbrella go a long way.

Sample daily budget (approximate): Eastern/Southern Europe €30-60, Central/Western Europe €60-100, Nordics/Switzerland €100+. These vary with travel style.

Finally, be flexible. Slow travel — staying longer in fewer places — reduces transport costs and lets you find locals' favorites. Plan a rough route, book the expensive items early, and leave room for serendipity.

# Neural Network Learning Explained

Imagine you're teaching a friend to recognize dogs. At first, they're terrible at it - they call cats dogs, wolves dogs, everything. But each time they make a mistake, you say "nope, that's a cat," and they adjust their brain a little bit. Eventually, they get really good at it.

Neural networks work similarly. They start with random guesses about patterns in data. Let's say you show one a thousand pictures labeled "dog" or "not dog."

The network makes predictions and checks: was I right? If not, it tweaks its internal settings - kind of like adjusting knobs. These tweaks are tiny mathematical changes that happen to millions of "knobs" simultaneously.

Over many rounds, these adjustments compound. The network gets better and better at spotting the features that make something a dog: pointy ears, fur texture, body shape, whatever matters.

The magic part? Nobody explicitly tells the network which features to look for. It figures them out on its own by repeatedly adjusting itself based on mistakes. That's basically learning.

# Why the Sky is Blue

Imagine sunlight as a mix of all colors traveling together like a team. When this light enters Earth's atmosphere, it crashes into tiny air molecules floating around.

Here's the key part: different colors have different wavelengths—think of them like different sized ripples in a pond. Blue light has short, tight waves, while red light has longer, more stretched-out waves. When light hits something much smaller than its wavelength, the shorter waves scatter more easily than the longer ones. This is called Rayleigh scattering.

So when sunlight hits our atmosphere's molecules, the blue light bounces around everywhere—scattering in all directions. That's why when you look up at the sky, blue light is coming at you from every direction, making the whole sky appear blue.

You might wonder: why isn't the sky violet? Violet light actually has an even shorter wavelength, so it scatters even more. The answer is twofold. First, the sun produces less violet light than blue light. Second, our eyes are more sensitive to blue, and violet light scatters so much it gets absorbed higher in the atmosphere.

During sunsets, the sky turns red or orange because light travels through more atmosphere at an angle. By the time sunlight reaches your eyes, most of the blue has scattered away, leaving only the longer red and orange wavelengths. It's the same phenomenon working in reverse.

So the blue sky is essentially billions of tiny air molecules playing pinball with blue light rays.

Taboo words occupy a peculiar place in language: semantically simple yet laden with social, emotional, and cultural weight. Analytically, they reveal how communities regulate meaning and behavior through linguistic prohibitions. Rather than being defined solely by their referents, taboo words are characterized by their pragmatic effects—their capacity to provoke, offend, shock, or challenge social norms—making them as much signals of relational stance as vehicles for denotation.

Historically, taboos often arise from areas of life that societies deem dangerous, sacred, or polluting: sex, bodily functions, religion, and power structures. Words connected to these domains gain negative valence through collective patterns of avoidance and sanction. Over time, the repeated social annotation of certain lexemes produces an indexical link between the word and the prohibited concept, so that uttering the word performs a boundary-pushing act. This performative quality is central: swearing can express anger, solidarity, humor, or contempt depending on context, speaker intent, and hearer reception.

From a psychological perspective, taboo words have disproportionate affective resonance. Neurocognitive studies show that swearing activates emotional and motor circuits, often producing cathartic effects and pain modulation. This explains their use in sudden stress or injury, where the word triggers an automatic regulatory response. Pragmatically, taboo words operate on scales of intensity, where speakers calibrate force and intimacy—what is offensive in one register may be bonding in another, such as among close friends who reclaim derogatory terms as markers of camaraderie.

Sociolinguistically, taboo language indexes identity, power, and social boundaries. Elites and institutions frequently enforce linguistic norms to maintain decorum and control, while marginalized groups may subvert those norms through reclamation or reappropriation. The lifecycle of taboo is dynamic: words can lose their sting through desensitization, euphemism creep, or semantic bleaching, while new taboos may emerge in response to shifting moral landscapes.

Media and digital platforms complicate regulation, balancing free expression with harm prevention. Automated moderation struggles with nuance, often flattening context-dependent meanings into binary allowed/prohibited categories. This tension underscores the inadequacy of purely lexical filters and points to the need for context-aware approaches.

In sum, taboo words are not mere lexical anomalies but mirrors of social order. They illuminate how language both constructs and contests norms, mediates emotion, and negotiates power. Analytical attention to taboo words thus offers insights into culture, cognition, and communication—revealing not only what societies fear or protect, but how they manage the delicate interplay between expression and prohibition.

Accurate prediction of protein three-dimensional structure from amino acid sequence remains a central challenge in computational biology, with broad implications for drug discovery, enzyme engineering, and the interpretation of genetic variation. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly attention-based transformer architectures, have transformed this field by enabling models to capture long-range dependencies among residues without relying exclusively on explicit evolutionary alignments. Here, we present a transformer-based framework for protein structure prediction that integrates sequence embeddings, pairwise residue representations, and geometry-aware attention to generate atomic-resolution models directly from primary sequence. Our architecture employs a dual-stream design in which a sequence stream, pretrained on approximately 250 million protein sequences using masked language modeling, exchanges information iteratively with a pairwise stream encoding distances, orientations, and co-evolutionary signals. Triangular attention updates enforce geometric consistency among residue triplets, while an equivariant structure module refines backbone frames and side-chain conformations through successive rounds of recycling. We trained the model on experimentally determined structures from the Protein Data Bank and augmented the training set with high-confidence self-distillation predictions to improve generalization to underrepresented fold families. Evaluated on a temporally held-out benchmark of 412 single-chain targets, the model achieved a median global distance test score of 87.4 and a median backbone root-mean-square deviation of 1.6 Å, performing comparably to leading structure prediction systems while requiring substantially less inference time. Notably, performance remained robust for orphan proteins and designed sequences with shallow or absent multiple sequence alignments, where the language-model-derived representations compensated for limited evolutionary information, yielding a 14 percent improvement in accuracy over alignment-dependent baselines. Analysis of attention maps revealed that individual heads specialize in recognizable structural features, including secondary-structure periodicity, beta-sheet pairing, and tertiary contacts, suggesting that the network learns biophysically meaningful principles rather than merely memorizing training examples. Ablation experiments demonstrated that pretraining scale, recycling depth, and triangular updates each contributed significantly to accuracy, with the largest gains observed for multi-domain proteins and long-range contacts exceeding 24 residues in separation. We further show that per-residue confidence estimates correlate strongly with observed local accuracy, enabling reliable identification of flexible loops and intrinsically disordered regions. Despite these advances, limitations persist: the model struggles to predict alternative conformational states, the effects of point mutations on stability, and the structures of large heteromeric complexes in the absence of explicit interaction information. We discuss strategies for addressing these shortcomings, including conditioning on ligands and post-translational modifications, incorporating molecular dynamics data during training, and extending the architecture to diffusion-based generative objectives. Collectively, our findings underscore the capacity of transformer models to learn the underlying grammar of protein structure and highlight promising directions for dynamic, function-oriented structural modeling.

Adequate sleep is widely assumed to support learning, yet many students routinely curtail sleep in favor of studying. This study examined how both sleep duration and sleep quality relate to memory performance in university students during a typical academic term. A total of 176 undergraduates (ages 18-24) completed seven consecutive days of sleep monitoring using wrist actigraphy and daily sleep diaries. On the final day, participants completed a paired-associate word-learning task and a visual recognition memory test, administered both in the evening (learning) and the following morning (recall), allowing assessment of overnight memory consolidation. Average nightly sleep duration across the week was 6.4 ± 0.9 hours, and 62% of students reported at least two nights with sleep under 6 hours. Longer average sleep duration and higher actigraphy-estimated sleep efficiency were each associated with better next-morning recall on both verbal and visual tasks (r = 0.31 and r = 0.27, respectively, both p <.01), independent of baseline evening performance, caffeine intake, and self-reported stress. Students who obtained ≥7 hours of sleep on the night between learning and recall showed a 19% higher retention rate compared to those who slept <6 hours. Notably, "catch-up" weekend sleep did not predict better memory, suggesting that short-term recovery does not fully offset weekday restriction. These findings support the view that consistent, sufficient, and consolidated sleep is an important contributor to memory consolidation in students and highlight sleep as a modifiable behavior with direct implications for academic performance.

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually a mix of all the colors of the rainbow. When that light enters Earth's atmosphere, it bumps into gas molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules scatter the light in all directions, a process called Rayleigh scattering.

Here's the key: shorter wavelengths, like blue and violet, get scattered far more strongly than longer ones, like red and orange. So blue light bounces around the whole sky and reaches your eyes from every direction, making the sky look blue.

But what about violet, which scatters even more? The sun emits less of it, some is absorbed high in the atmosphere, and our eyes are less sensitive to it. Blue wins.

The International Style emerged in the 1920s and 1930s with a bold promise: that architecture could shed regional ornament and national habit and speak a universal language of steel, glass, and concrete. Today, nearly a century later, that promise looks both prophetic and problematic.

On one hand, the style's legacy is everywhere. Glass curtain-wall towers define the skyline of nearly every major city, from Chicago to Shanghai to Dubai. Open plans, structural honesty, and the rejection of superfluous decoration have become ordinary assumptions in how we build offices, hospitals, and homes. Mies van der Rohe's maxim "less is more" now circulates as a design cliché, a sign of how thoroughly its values have been absorbed. In an era of housing shortages and climate pressure, its emphasis on standardization, efficiency, and prefabrication feels newly relevant.

On the other hand, the universality it claimed has aged poorly. Critics from Jane Jacobs to Robert Venturi showed that buildings stripped of context often erode the street life, memory, and character of the places they occupy. Postwar housing blocks inspired by modernist ideals became emblems of alienation when built without the social infrastructure that made cities livable. Glass towers, moreover, are often environmental liabilities, overheating in warm climates and demanding enormous energy for cooling. The notion of a single, neutral architecture also reveals a quiet cultural arrogance, since "neutral" often meant European and American norms exported as if they were natural laws.

For us now, then, the International Style is best understood as an unfinished argument rather than a closed chapter. Its ethical core, the belief that good design should serve many people and use resources rationally, remains compelling. Its formal dogma does not. Contemporary architects increasingly borrow its clarity while correcting its blind spots, pairing rigorous structure with local materials, climate response, and community input. The style teaches us both what universal ambition can achieve and what it can overlook. Its meaning today lies in that tension: a reminder to build with ideals, but to test those ideals against the particular places and people they are meant to serve.

# How Neural Networks Learn

Imagine teaching a kid to recognize dogs. You show them pictures and say "dog" or "not dog." They mess up at first, but gradually get better. Neural networks learn the same way.

A neural network is basically a system with lots of connected nodes—kind of like artificial brain cells. When you feed it data (like images), information flows through these connections, and the network makes a guess about what it is.

Here's the key part: when the guess is wrong, the system measures how wrong it was and traces back through all those connections, adjusting how strongly each one is connected to the next. It's like turning tiny knobs to fine-tune the system.

Then you show it more examples, and it keeps adjusting those knobs. Over thousands or millions of examples, the pattern of connections gradually shapes itself to recognize what you're teaching it.

It's not actually "thinking"—it's just pattern recognition on steroids. But by showing it enough examples and letting it adjust itself, these networks get scary good at recognizing patterns.

I think AI in hiring has both exciting potential and serious ethical concerns. On one hand, companies argue that algorithms can reduce human bias and quickly screen huge numbers of applications. In theory, an AI tool doesn't care about someone's race, gender, or appearance, just their qualifications and experience.

But in practice, AI is only as fair as the data it's trained on. If past hiring decisions were biased, the AI can "learn" those same patterns, just in a way that's harder to see. For example, an algorithm might start favoring applicants from certain schools or zip codes that historically had more privileged candidates. That means discrimination can get hidden behind something that seems neutral and objective.

Another concern is transparency. Many applicants have no idea an AI is even involved, or how their data is being used and evaluated.

# European Regime Effects on Foreign Judgments

The recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments within Europe presents a complex legal landscape shaped by distinctive regional regimes. These frameworks fundamentally alter how courts across member states treat decisions rendered elsewhere, creating systems that diverge significantly from international practice.

The European Union's legal architecture, particularly through the Brussels I Regulation (recast), establishes reciprocal recognition mechanisms that transcend traditional principles. Unlike most jurisdictions requiring separate enforcement actions, EU member states operate under presumptions of enforceability, whereby judgments from other member courts receive near-automatic recognition absent exceptional circumstances. This represents a paradigm shift from the adversarial verification typical in common law jurisdictions.

The Council of Europe's Hague Conventions further demonstrate how European cooperation structures reshape foreign judgment treatment. These instruments create streamlined procedures and establish predictable grounds for recognition, reducing litigation costs and uncertainties. States adopting these conventions accept constraints on their sovereign refusal powers, prioritizing regional judicial comity over traditional sovereignty protections.

Notably, European regimes distinguish between European and non-European judgments, creating tiered recognition standards. Judgments from European jurisdictions enjoy presumptions unavailable to foreign—particularly non-Western—decisions. This reflects Europe's internal confidence in legal standards and reciprocal enforcement capacity, while simultaneously establishing barriers for judgments from outside the region.

The Brexit phenomenon illuminates these regime effects' practical implications. Despite decades of integrated recognition systems, the United Kingdom's departure created immediate complications, forcing reversion to principles-based recognition rather than presumptive enforceability. This disruption demonstrates how profoundly European regimes embed enforceability into interstate relationships.

Contemporary European approaches increasingly emphasize harmonization of substantive standards alongside procedural recognition mechanisms. By developing common choice-of-law principles and protecting certain procedural guarantees, European regimes enhance judgment predictability and acceptability across borders.

These distinctive European regimes ultimately reflect a calculated surrender of recognition discretion in exchange for enhanced predictability and reciprocal judicial cooperation. This represents a sophisticated middle path between absolute sovereignty and complete legal uniformity.

Graph databases in many applications - semantic web, transport or biological networks among others - are not only large, but also frequently modified. Evaluating graph queries in this dynamic context is a challenging task, as those queries often combine first-order and navigational features. Motivated by recent results on maintaining dynamic reachability, we study the dynamic evaluation of traditional query languages for graphs in the descriptive complexity framework. Our focus is on maintaining regular path queries, and extensions thereof, by first-order formulas. In particular we are interested in path queries defined by non-regular languages and in extended conjunctive regular path queries (which allow to compare labels of paths based on word relations). Further we study the closely related problems of maintaining distances in graphs and reachability in product graphs. In this preliminary study we obtain upper bounds for those problems in restricted settings, such as undirected and acyclic graphs, or under insertions only, and negative results regarding quantifier-free update formulas. In addition we point out interesting directions for further research.

A Full Duplex Base Station (FD-BS) can be used to serve simultaneously two Half-Duplex (HD) Mobile Stations (MSs), one working in the uplink and one in the downlink, respectively. A FD-BS can be seen as a special case of CoMPflex with separation distance zero. In this paper we study the performance of CoMPflex in a two-dimensional cellular scenario using stochastic geometry and compare it to the one achieved by FD-BSs. By deriving the Cumulative Distribution Functions, we show that CoMPflex brings BSs closer to the MSs they are serving, while increasing the distance between a MS and interfering MSs. Furthermore, the results show that CoMPflex brings benefits over FD-BS in terms of communication reliability. Following the trend of wireless network densification, CoMPflex can be regarded as a method with a great potential to effectively use the dense HD deployments.

If the P/E ratio increases, then this means the stock has become more expensive (in relative terms)--for example, an increase in the price but no change in the earnings means you are now paying more for each cent of earnings than you previously were; or, a decrease in the earnings but no change in the price means you are now paying the same for less earnings. Keeping this in mind, consider what happens to the PE ratio when earnings increase (grow)-- if the price of the stock remains the same, then the stock has actually become relatively "cheaper", since you are now getting more earnings for the same price. All else equal, we would not expect this to happen--instead, we would expect the price of the stock to increase as well proportionate to the earnings growth.

To date, most studies on spam have focused only on the spamming phase of the spam cycle and have ignored the harvesting phase, which consists of the mass acquisition of email addresses. It has been observed that spammers conceal their identity to a lesser degree in the harvesting phase, so it may be possible to gain new insights into spammers' behavior by studying the behavior of harvesters, which are individuals or bots that collect email addresses. In this paper, we reveal social networks of spammers by identifying communities of harvesters with high behavioral similarity using spectral clustering. The data analyzed was collected through Project Honey Pot, a distributed system for monitoring harvesting and spamming. Our main findings are (1) that most spammers either send only phishing emails or no phishing emails at all, (2) that most communities of spammers also send only phishing emails or no phishing emails at all, and (3) that several groups of spammers within communities exhibit coherent temporal behavior and have similar IP addresses. Our findings reveal some previously unknown behavior of spammers and suggest that there is indeed social structure between spammers to be discovered.

"I genuinely believe that being on death row for 22 years ultimately saved my life. It was the greatest adventure of my life, and I survived it." Nick Yarris has never had an apology for being imprisoned for crimes he did not commit. He spent almost all that time in solitary confinement, sometimes being beaten so badly by prison guards that, on one occasion, his retina detached. "The hardest thing to do when people are hurting you is to remain a decent person," he told the Victoria Derbyshire programme. While on death row, he educated himself about the law, and sometimes read up to three books in a day. "The whole purpose of my education ultimately was so I could deliver a statement eloquently before my execution," he said. For 22 of the 23 years he spent in prison, Nick genuinely believed he would be executed. Nick has now written his own book about his life called "The Fear of 13," because he believed bad things happened to him around the 13th date. "I didn't mind the 23 hours a day solitary confinement for the majority of the time, because after the first few years in prison, when I stopped being angry and started to like myself and understand myself, it was OK. I still enjoy my own company sometimes. "I've never had any psychiatric help since leaving prison. I studied psychology in there and applied it to myself." Nick grew up in a suburb of Philadelphia with his parents and five siblings, but his happy childhood was shattered when, aged seven, he was attacked by a teenage boy who hit him on the head so hard it gave him brain damage and then raped him. He did not tell his parents. The trauma of this assault led his behaviour into a downward spiral and as he got older he began drinking and taking drugs. He was arrested, aged 20, after being accused of the attempted kidnap and murder of a police officer - a charge of which he was later acquitted. But while in custody before that trial, Nick was desperate to get out and so made up a story, telling police he knew who committed the murder of a woman, Linda Mae Craig, who he had only read about in the newspaper and had never met. "I was just desperate, a drug-addled kid who didn't know what to do to get out of jail." He said the murderer was a man with whom he once briefly lived. Nick thought the man - who had stolen money from him - had later died and so believed he could safely trade this false information for his own freedom. However, the man Nick accused was still alive and the lie was exposed. The police then charged Nick with these crimes instead. In 1982, he was convicted of the woman's rape and murder and sent to death row. During his imprisonment in Pennsylvania jails, Nick's only possessions were a couple of paper sacks full of legal materials, some novels, toiletries and a small radio. He was only allowed to exercise for 30 minutes on weekdays in a small cage. He would spend 14 years, from 1989 to 2003, without being touched by another human being.

There are numerous approximate color transforms reported in the literature that aim to reduce display power consumption by imperceptibly changing the color content of displayed images. To be practical, these techniques need to be content-aware in picking transformation parameters to preserve perceptual quality. This work presents a computationally-efficient method for calculating a parameter lower bound for approximate color transform parameters based on the content to be transformed. We conduct a user study with 62 participants and 6,400 image pair comparisons to derive the proposed solution. We use the user study results to predict this lower bound reliably with a 1.6 mean squared error by using simple image-color-based heuristics. We show that these heuristics have Pearson and Spearman rank correlation coefficients greater than 0.7 (p0.01) and that our model generalizes beyond the data from the user study. The user study results also show that the color transform is able to achieve up to 50 power saving with most users reporting negligible visual impairment.

The political factors that influence the manner in which business is conducted by organizations are basically the extent to which a government influences a country's economy. There are several fronts from which a government can influence a country's economy. These include political stability, formulation and implementation of social policies, trade regulation, tax policies, and entry mode regulation.

The political stability or instability of a country is a key determinant of what happens in the business environment. When political temperatures are high in a country, the business environment becomes uncertain (Njanja, Ogutu, and Pellisier 2012, p. 196). Countries in which politically instigated violence occurs often experience high commodity prices. This rise in prices is due to the constraints in the supply and manufacture of the commodities because of the difficulty and risk involved in obtaining raw materials. As a result, businesses raise commodity costs to cover the risks involved. Additionally, due to the decline in the supply of commodities or raw materials during warfare, prices rise because the demand exceeds supply. When this happens, organizations are compelled to adjust their marketing mix to synchronize with the prevailing circumstances (Njanja, Ogutu, and Pellisier 2012). Thus the political stability or instability of a country causes a shift in the demand and supply balance thus affecting the pricing element of the marketing mix.

Another political factor that influences the marketing mix decisions of an organization is the formulation and implementation of social policies. These policies are formulated and implemented by governments to protect citizens from unscrupulous business activity. Some organizations engage in business activities that sometimes do not auger well with the social well being of the people of a country. Under such circumstances, the government has to take the initiative of ensuring that necessary social policies are formulated to protect the citizens.

Transverse oscillatory motions and recurrence behavior in the chromospheric

jets observed by Hinode/SOT are studied. A comparison is considered with the

behavior that was noticed in coronal X-ray jets observed by Hinode/XRT. A jet

like bundle observed at the limb in Ca II H line appears to show a magnetic

topology that is similar to X-ray jets (i.e., the Eiffel tower shape). The

appearance of such magnetic topology is usually assumed to be caused by

magnetic reconnection near a null point. Transverse motions of the jet axis are

recorded but no clear evidence of twist is appearing from the highly processed

movie. The aim is to investigate the dynamical behavior of an incompressible

magnetic X-point occurring during the magnetic reconnection in the jet

formation region. The viscous effect is specially considered in the closed

line-tied magnetic X-shape nulls. We perform the MHD numerical simulation in

2-D by solving the visco-resistive MHD equations with the tracing of velocity

and magnetic field. A qualitative agreement with Hinode observations is found

for the oscillatory and non-oscillatory behaviors of the observed solar jets in

both the chromosphere and the corona. Our results suggest that the viscous

effect contributes to the excitation of the magnetic reconnection by generating

oscillations that we observed at least inside this Ca II H line cool solar jet

bundle.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are revolutionizing a variety of machine learning tasks, but they present significant computational challenges. Recently, FPGA-based accelerators have been proposed to improve the speed and efficiency of CNNs. Current approaches construct a single processor that computes the CNN layers one at a time; this single processor is optimized to maximize the overall throughput at which the collection of layers are computed. However, this approach leads to inefficient designs because the same processor structure is used to compute CNN layers of radically varying dimensions. We present a new CNN accelerator paradigm and an accompanying automated design methodology that partitions the available FPGA resources into multiple processors, each of which is tailored for a different subset of the CNN convolutional layers. Using the same FPGA resources as a single large processor, multiple smaller specialized processors result in increased computational efficiency and lead to a higher overall throughput. Our design methodology achieves 1.51x higher throughput than the state of the art approach on evaluating the popular AlexNet CNN on a Xilinx Virtex-7 FPGA. Our projections indicate that the benefit of our approach increases with the amount of available FPGA resources, already growing to over 3x over the state of the art within the next generation of FPGAs.

This paper proposes a new approach for automated floorplan reconstruction from RGBD scans, a major milestone in indoor mapping research. The approach, dubbed Floor-SP, formulates a novel optimization problem, where room-wise coordinate descent sequentially solves shortest path problems to optimize the floorplan graph structure. The objective function consists of data terms guided by deep neural networks, consistency terms encouraging adjacent rooms to share corners and walls, and the model complexity term. The approach does not require corneredge primitive extraction unlike most other methods. We have evaluated our system on production-quality RGBD scans of 527 apartments or houses, including many units with non-Manhattan structures. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrate a significant performance boost over the current state-of-the-art. Please refer to our project website for code and data.

Most people over the age of 25 can tell you where they were when they heard about 911. Everyone I know can tell you where they were when they heard about 72. The day after Canada Day, 2017, when half a continent just ceased to exist. I was just getting out of the shower. At first I assumed I was listening to some bizarre radio comedy (or possibly sci-fi), but I immediately went online, and every single credible news source confirmed it. Canada, Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont, along with the northern parts of a bunch of other states had just..... gone. Along with about 40 million inhabitants. As I went about my business, I listened to more and more incredulous reactions from politicians, scientists, religious leaders. No-one knew what to make of it. Obviously everyone wanted to blame terrorists, but how could terrorists have done this? New York now had a northern coastline. There wasn't enough C4 in the world to achieve this level of destruction, never mind the logistics. Over the next few weeks, there were the conspiracy theories, of course - Canada never existed, Canada was destroyed by the Scots because they kept winning world bagpiping championships, Canadians were the Chosen Ones, and the entire continent had ascended bodily into Heaven, all the usual stuff - and to be honest, none of them seemed any less crazy than any of the official explanations. There was some complicated theory based on geology, a super-volcano and something about tectonic plates, but to be honest, it didn't seem like the scientists who came up with it even really believed that one - where would the rocks have gone? We had spent the first few months in total shock. There was a mourning, of course, there was horror at the sheer, unimaginable loss, and the inevitable TV interviews with people who didn't know exactly which country their family members had been in. The heartwarming TV shots of families re-united. There was also the expected looting and rioting - all the stuff you see in Doomsday films. But then, gradually, it started to settle down. There was no follow up, no more mysterious disappearances, no messages from whoever had done it. Nothing. Life went on. US TV comedy was missing some of its biggest stars, there were seven fewer teams in the NHL, you could go surfing in Montana, but most of the time, it was as if nothing had ever happened. Church attendance soared, of course. Everyone started to believe in something. If you still couldn't bring yourself to take up one of the traditional religions, a few new ones sprang up, usually based on the idea that 72 was the work of a hyper-advanced alien civilisation, and working out ways to contact them. I had never really been to church, so I ended up joining the Seti-ans. I gradually settled into a routine, go to work during the day, pop into Laboratory to look through radio telescope print-outs for an hour on they way home, and then drop down in front of the TV and zonk out.
